**Surah 70: Sa'ala (also called al-Ma'arij)**

[p. 386] Its central theme is the affirmation of the Resurrection (qiyamah) and the warning to those who disbelieve in it. It portrays its greatness through the greatness of its dominion and the length of its Day, and it consoles the one who warns of it, by showing what awaits those who denied him: humiliation, abasement, and ruin. It indicates that its occurrence is necessary, by ending the preceding surah with its name, al-Haqqah ("The Inevitable Reality"), as a reminder that it is unavoidable and that there is no escape from it. It also indicates this through His power, mentioned at the beginning; His knowledge, mentioned in the middle; and His exaltation above the deficiency of neglecting it, mentioned at the end. It is no secret that He informed us that He sent all His messengers to warn of it. He sent Noah, peace be upon him, in the earliest age, as He mentioned in his own surah, when people differed after they had been upon agreement on the true religion in the time of their father Adam, peace and blessings be upon him, and split into those who affirmed and those who denied. From this it is known that those who came after him are more deserving of this warning, being closer to it. He followed this announcement by stating that he called the jinn to it, whose path concerning it was the path of humankind. [He followed that -] after the sending of the first messengers to it, in time, the last of them in time and the first of them in prophethood, when he was a prophet while Adam was between spirit and body. He began with the surah al-Muzzammil, concerning his prophethood, his elevated purification, sanctification and exaltation, the report of his mission, and the warning against opposing him. He followed this with the warning of the Resurrection by proclaiming the message and erasing every error. When his prophethood was established and his mission was confirmed in the most beautiful, clearest, most manifest, highest and most excellent manner, [p. 387] He, glorified be He, made the entire surah of al-Qiyamah (The Resurrection) about it, as an announcement that the matter is [great -] very great, requiring care, preparation, and striving with utmost strength and full effort. Then He followed this with al-Insan (Man), as an indication that the human being is the ultimate purpose of existence. It is therefore not fitting, in wisdom, that He should leave him aimless. He explained many of its conditions. Then in al-Mursalat He swore that its coming is a truth that cannot be avoided and from which there is no escape. Then in ʿamma He marvelled [at them -] at their questioning about it and their wonder at it. Then He swore by its turmoil in al-Nazi'at, and depicted aspects of its matter and its terrors as He willed. Then in ʿabasa He gave precedence to the indication that some people have had their hearts sealed, so there is no remedy for their affirming it, even though what has been made clear in the preceding surah and others regarding its matter. Then He depicted it in "Idha al-shamsu kuwwirat" (al-Takwir) with a depiction such that it becomes as if seen with one's own eyes; had the veil been lifted, those who were certain of it would not have increased in certainty. Then in al-Infitar He explained that matters in it are not according to the ordinary course of affairs; rather all causes are severed and all lineages are abolished, and everyone is submissive, humbled and reverent. The greatest of them in worldly arrogance will be the most abased and regretful there. Then He followed this with those who deserve shackles, chains and fetters there. Then He gave the highest rank to the people of faith, whom He disposed to acknowledge it and recognize it. This continued to the end of the Qur'an. Hardly does any surah come without knowing it to the utmost degree of knowledge, up to the end, where your closing with "al-Din" (The Religion) is an indication that knowing it is the religion. [p. 388] He pointed to it in "Tabbat" and followed it with al-Ikhlas (Sincerity), indicating that none will be safe in it except the monotheists, protected from manifest and hidden trials, characterized by great and abundant praiseworthy qualities. This indicates that the greatest aim of the Qur'an concerns its supremely important matter, for there is no book after this Book to be awaited, and no nation more honoured than this one, singled out with an explanation greater than its explanation. This is one of the aspects by which the Qur'an surpassed the earlier books and the scriptures that existed in the past centuries. It also indicates that the matter has drawn near, the terror has struck, and fear has kindled, so that those who are concerned will strive for deliverance from its punishment and escape, when there is no flight, no refuge, and "no time for escape" (lata hina manas). We ask God for well-being on its Day and a pleasing life. This aim is indicated by its name "Sa'ala," and likewise by al-Ma'arij (The Ascending Stairways), which are the most suitable of its features for indicating this. May God, glorified and exalted be He, protect us from its calamities and ruins. Amen.

(In the name of God, the Sovereign, the Greatest, before whose loftiness necks and hopes fall short; the Merciful, who made manifest the blessing of clear expression, spread it and made it famous, until it became so clear that no one has any hope of claiming its obscurity; the Merciful, who chose from among His servants those whom He enabled to understand Him and to obey Him, so they became His friends.)

* *

[p. 389] When He had concluded the matter of the Great Catastrophe in al-Haqqah, until its matter was established, and its secret and its open were made equal, and He indicated it so that no kind of confusion remained regarding the necessity, in wisdom, of distinguishing between the doer of good and the doer of evil, and concluded that abandoning this is contrary to perfection in what we perceive of the affairs of workers, after He had informed that He knows that among them are deniers, and since the questioner about something indicates that the questioner did not understand it as it should be understood, nor truly possessed its real knowledge, He marvelled at the beginning of this surah at those who asked about it, saying: ﴿A questioner asked﴾. This indicates that even if only one of the servants had asked about it, he would have been deserving of wonder and reproach by singling him out, in His saying: ﴿a questioner﴾ (sa'il). It comes from the root "su'al" (asking), in the reading of the one who lightened it by replacing the hamzah with an alif, and from hamz (the pronunciation with hamzah).

Since their questioning about the time of the Hour and the punishment, and their demand to hasten it, was only mockery, He embedded "sa'ala" with the sense of mockery. Then He omitted it and indicated it by a state He extracted from it and omitted, and indicated it by what He governed with the verb, saying. Or He omitted the object of the transitive verb of asking, which is "ʿan" (about), so that it would include every thing asked about, as an indication that whoever reflects upon the primordial nature (fitrah) and what it calls to of perfection, and obeys it, becoming a Muslim, will be showered with knowledge, and the rays of understanding will shine upon him in its manifestations. Thus He clarified the intended meaning of the text by His saying: ﴿with a punishment﴾, that is, about the Day of Resurrection, [by a cause of -] [p. 390] punishment, or mocking, with a very great punishment ﴿that is to befall﴾. He expressed it with the lam (li) as derision from them, like His saying: ﴿so give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 24], and so He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 2:

﴿For the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those firmly established in this description. The meaning is: if there is anything [for them -] in the Hereafter, it is the punishment. The reading of Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir with the lightening of the hamza [is more -] expressive of wonder, i.e., his mouth gushed forth with speech and his lips moved with it, because, alongside its being said "sāla yasʾalu" (to ask), like "khāfa yakhāfu" (to fear), a dialect form for the hamzated verb, it may be from "saʾala yasʾalu" (to ask). Al-Baghawi said: This is because the people of Makkah, when the Prophet ﷺ warned them of the punishment, said: "Concerning whom is this punishment, and for whom is it? Ask about it," so it was revealed.

When He informed of the inevitability of its occurrence, He gave the reason for it with His saying: ﴿There is no one who can avert it﴾, i.e., in any way or by any stratagem, ﴿from God﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 3], i.e., the Supreme King, to whom there is no equal, so no one has any command along with Him. And when there is no averter of it from Him, there is no averter of it from anyone else. Its promise has already been made, wisdom has indicated it, so its occurrence is certain and its reversal is impossible.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 3:

Since the One who has power is described as exalted, and the one who is powerless is described as low and near the bottom, and since that by which one ascends to the high is called a daraj (ascent, staircase) and that by which one descends to the lowest is called a dark (descent), and since all places are of equal standing in relation to Him, glorified is He, the expression chosen was one that indicates height, which is used as a metaphor for power and greatness. So He said, describing Him in a way that suits being an indication of the reason: ﴿Lord of the ascending stairways﴾ (p. 391), meaning the degrees that have no end at all, by what the form of the plural of the highest plural pattern indicates, and this is a metaphor for exaltation. It was named thus because the one ascending a staircase resembles the gait of a lame man. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that they are the heavens. And it indicates, along with what the abundance of these degrees indicates, the wondrous power in facilitating them for the angels, by His saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 4:

﴿The angels ascend﴾ i.e., and they are the most powerful of creation and the most capable of piercing the heavens' layers and of swiftness in passing through them, to the extent that they are faster than the flash of the glittering lightning. ﴿And the Spirit﴾ i.e., Jibril (upon him be peace), singled out for his honour; or it is a creation greater than the angels. It was also said: it is the spirit of the believing servant when it is taken at death. ﴿To Him﴾ i.e., the place of His communion and the furthest limit of elevation possible for His creatures. It is connected either to the ascending, or to the content of His saying ﴿in a day﴾, i.e., of your days, in which is ﴿fifty thousand﴾ of ... [the text reads: "فِيهِ آدَمِيًّا"] — in it, measured in human (terms), ﴿fifty thousand﴾, and He explained the hardship of its ascent, or of being in it if the Resurrection is intended, by saying ﴿year﴾ and not saying "a year," for example. It is also permissible that this day be a time frame for the punishment, so the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection; and that its length for the disbeliever be considered in terms of the distress that reaches him because of the intensity of the terrors upon him, since it has been reported that it will be made light for the believer ﴿until it is as long as a single prayer﴾ — end.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) that the meaning is: if someone other than Allah were in charge of the reckoning, he would not finish it except in this measure, whereas He, glorified is He, finishes it in half a day of the days of this world. Mujahid, al-Hakam and 'Ikrimah said: it is the age of the world from its beginning to its end, fifty thousand years, and none of you knows how much has passed or how much remains except Allah. What is beneficial here has already passed in the commentary on Surat "Alif Lam Mim al-Sajda."

When all of this was a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ regarding their hastening of the punishment, mocking and denying it, whether the aim is to depict its greatness or the punishment itself, its consequence was His saying: ﴿So be patient﴾, that is, over their harm, and this patience must not be separated from conveying the message to them, for you have come close to the time of retribution against them, O Opener and Sealer, you to whom I did not make clear to anyone what I made clear through his tongue. Patience (al-sabr) is restraining the self from what is disliked, whether in advancing or in holding back. Its beauty lies in the outward calm that comes from steadfastness and the inward calm that comes from knowledge ('irfan, knowledge of God), ﴿a beautiful patience﴾, that is, one not mixed with any agitation, [no -] impatience, complaint, or haste. For their punishment and your victory over them are due to the greatness of the One who sent you, so it must necessarily occur, because denying it and rejecting it amounts to a denial of Him. This was before the command to fight.

(p-393) The Imam Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: When Surah al-Haqqah concluded with the most severe and greatest threat [of punishment], he followed it with a response to those who were slow to accept that and considered it remote, since this is something the obstinate and the skeptical tend to resort to. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿A seeker asked for a punishment that is about to befall﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 1], up to His saying ﴿They see it as far off﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 6-7]. Then He described their state at that time: ﴿The guilty one would wish he could ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], and so on. Then He followed this by stating that such ransom would not avail him ﴿Indeed, it is the Blaze﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 15]. Then the surah was concluded with an emphatic confirmation of the warning and a stronger threat: ﴿So leave them to wade in their vain talk and to play﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 42], up to His saying ﴿That is the Day they were promised﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 44]. That is the Day of al-Haqqah and the Day of al-Qari'ah. [End of quotation.]

Since His being, exalted is He, is established in greatness, as shown earlier, by the effects that manifest in this existence and what it contains, and since their considering what He reported to be far off was a weak, feeble, and trivial claim that could hardly be believed, [it is evident that] anyone would try to refute these matters, which are as clear as the sun with no concealment or ambiguity at all, by such a claim. He said, emphasizing: ﴿Indeed, they﴾, meaning the disbelievers who deny and seek hastening [of the punishment], ﴿see it﴾, meaning that Day, which is long, or its punishment, ﴿as far off﴾, meaning the time of its occurrence, because they regard it as impossible or act as those who consider it remote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 7:

﴿And We see it﴾, by reason of the majesty We possess, which decreed its existence, and it is easy for Us, ﴿nearby﴾. Whether by this is meant nearness in time or nearness in place, it is easy [for Our power], and it is certainly coming, and everything that is coming is near, and the distant and the near are on an equal footing with Us.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 70, Verse 8:**

When He had mentioned, concerning this Day, what would prompt questioning about it, He resumed explaining it, showing its greatness, so He said: ﴿On the Day﴾, meaning it will occur when ﴿the sky will be﴾ [i.e. -] the one that is the firmest and most solid of what you see, because of the greatness of the terrors that will occur in it, ﴿like molten metal﴾, meaning like a melted substance from ores, in a state of... or the sediment of olive oil.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 9:

﴿And the mountains will be﴾ those which are the hardest of the earth and the heaviest of what is in it, ﴿like wool﴾, i.e., dyed wool of various colours, carded, which the wind scatters like floating dust. This is because the mountains are, in their original state, of various colours, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And among the mountains are streaks, white and red﴾ [Fatir: 27], and so on. Al-Baghawi said: "The term ʿihn (wool) is applied only to dyed wool." He said: "The first stage of the mountains' change is that they become crumbled sand, then carded wool, then scattered dust [then dust –] dispersed." – End.

{Wa-la yas'alu} [i.e., "and no close friend will ask"] {hamimun hamiman} — from the intensity of the terrors, a close friend (ḥamīm) — that is, one who is extremely close and intimate — will not ask a close friend like himself about anything, because of the excessive preoccupations. Moreover, He has revealed to them that no soul will avail another soul in anything, and that the means have been severed and lineages have vanished, when He has exposed the trial, that there is no honor except through piety. This is according to the reading of the majority (al-Jamā'ah) with a fatḥah on the yā' [yubṣarūnahum], and according to the reading of Ibn Kathīr with the passive voice (al-binā' lil-maf'ūl) [yubṣarūnahum / yas'alu]. The meaning is that no one will be held accountable for another, as some rulers in this world impose on the relatives of one whom he has brought near, because He has no need of that, since His power encompasses all things equally.

Since the absence of questioning may be because some of them do not see one another, due to the great number gathered, the intense crush, and people being scattered in it according to the ranks of their deeds, he resumed with the answer for one who seems to say: "Perhaps that is left aside because they do not see them?" So he said, using the passive form and the intensive verb form (tafʿīl, the doubling of the middle radical that signals intensity) to indicate the greatness of that "making them see" and its departure from custom, and in the plural, because what is meant by the close friend (ḥamīm) is the category, and the plural is more indicative of the generality of the "making them see." Al-Baghawi said: "There is no created being on the Day of Resurrection but that he is placed before the eyes of his companion, from among the jinn and mankind." End of quote. The wisdom in this is that it indicates more clearly the severing of all means, so that none of them asks the other about anything of his affairs, because each is preoccupied with himself. Thus the absence of questioning is not due to concealment but to preoccupation, and each person is concerned with what he has. ﴿They will be shown to them﴾, i.e., a seer will see them, so no one is hidden from anyone, even if his place is distant, and each flees from the other because of his preoccupation with himself. When the report of the greatness of that day reached a point that hearts cannot bear, he mentioned its result, resuming: ﴿The guilty one would love﴾ [al-Hijr: 2], i.e., wishes and desires, ﴿the guilty one﴾, i.e., this category, whether he is a disbeliever or a disobedient Muslim who knows that he will be punished for his disobedience. It was restricted to him because the obedient Muslim (p-396) will intercede for whomever he is permitted to, and nothing of that troubles him. This wish is shown to be a mere longing by his saying: ﴿if he could ransom himself﴾, i.e., his own self, ﴿from the punishment of that day﴾, i.e., a day when these terrors are with the person most dear to his heart and nearest to him, let alone that he should ask about his circumstances.

Since the context is that of ransom, he began with those most dear to him in that regard, unlike what comes in ʿAbasa (Surah 80), so he said: ﴿with his children﴾, because of the severity of what he sees.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 12:

When He mentioned the people closest to the heart and most dear of those who would stand by him for his support and defense, He followed it with what comes next in rank and affection, and for whom ransoming oneself is, especially among the Arabs, among the worst of shames. So He said: ﴿And his wife﴾, that is, his spouse, whom it is incumbent upon him to defend and to remain always with, because she is the equal of his soul in this world.

When He mentioned the spouse, given the completeness of the bond she has, He followed her with the brother (al-shaqiq), whose defense does not carry the same obligation as the defense of the womenfolk (al-harim), and who may perhaps be estranged. So He said: ﴿And his brother﴾.

and his close kin (fasilatihi), meaning his clan (ʿashirah), those nearest to him among those who are separated from him (fuṣila ʿanhu), ﴿who shelters him﴾, that is, who takes him into their fold in times of hardship and protects him, because he is the closest of people to them and the dearest to them, so they are the greatest of people in their right over him and the most precious to him.

When this verse concerned the ransom, he placed first the one farthest from that, then the farther, in terms of benefit and disgrace. When the verse of ʿAbasa (80:34-37) concerned flight and aversion, he placed the closest first, then the closer, and the most intimate in companionship, then the more intimate.

When he particularized here, he generalized, saying: ﴿and whoever is on the earth﴾, meaning of the two weighty ones (al-thaqalayn, humankind and jinn) and others, whether among them is a friend from whom one cannot bear to be parted and must have in every case, or not. Since this might be particularized to someone other than him, he said, confirming the intended literal sense of "min" (of/from): ﴿all of them﴾.

When a person has the matters uncovered for him there, that is, they are revealed, and they become manifest to him in the fullest manifestation, the Exalted said: ﴿So today your sight is sharp﴾ (Qaf 50:22). Thus he knows that nothing will save him from the encompassing and ruinous sins. He indicated the improbability by the particle of distance, and said, conjoining it to "yaftadi" (he would ransom himself): ﴿then it would deliver him﴾, that is, then he would wish that by that there could be for him a salvation renewed for him at some time or other.

Since this [ mimmā - ] is something one may hope for salvation from, and since some people have a seal set upon their hearts, so that their desires lead them astray until they consider the impossible possible, He said, expressing it through the gathering of deterrents and the sharp reproaches: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning let there be a deterrence for the criminal (p-398), meaning a deterrence from this affection of his, and let its effect follow upon him, for that will never happen in any way whatsoever.

Since the use of a pronoun before its antecedent (al-iḍmār qabla al-dhikr) is for magnifying the referent of that pronoun within the context in which it stands, because it signals that it is ever present in the mind and never absent at all, given the great significance the context carries, He said after this great deterrence from salvation, indeed from wishing for it: ﴿Indeed it﴾, that is, the Fire, which is the whip of the King prepared for whoever disobeys Him, threatened in this context with its punishment, and which takes hold of him so that it becomes his prison: ﴿a blazing fire﴾, that is, possessing pure flame, extremely hot, flaring up, meaning it blazes, so that some of it devours other parts when it finds nothing else to eat, and devours whatever it finds, whatever that may be.

﴿Nazzā'ah lil-shawā﴾ (a fierce puller): that is, it is intensely pulling at the scalps, so how much more so at other skin. He said in al-Qamus: "al-shawa: the two hands and the two feet, the extremities, the top of the skull, and whatever is not a fatal spot — end of quote." It is also said: "and all the skin and flesh; it pulls these off, then they return as they were in that moment, so that they may experience the torment which they used to deny in themselves at every instant."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 17:

Since escape is not possible from the One who calls, who is able to bring about the summoning, He figuratively expressed their being brought forth and drawn to them by His saying: ﴿She calls﴾. It is also possible that this is literal, so that she says in her calling to herself: "Come to me, O polytheist! Come to me, O hypocrite!" and the like. Then she gathers them up as a bird gathers grain. ﴿Whoever﴾, that is, every person, ﴿turned his back﴾, that is, among the jinn and mankind, that is, whoever from them turned away, when it was his duty to turn towards it; whether that turning away was from it (the Fire) or from the deeds that are suited to delivering one from it. Since turning away may come from an overpowering natural disposition, so that its doer is counted among those who may be excused, he made clear that the matter is not like that, and said: ﴿and turned away﴾, that is, he imposed upon his original, upright nature the turning away from the means of salvation.

Since this world and the Hereafter are rival co-wives, turning toward one of them signifies turning away from the other, so (the verse) says, indicating by it his turning his back with his heart: ﴿And he gathered﴾, that is, everything that was attributed to this world.

Since it is the customary way that whoever has this world as his greatest concern will have his concern in gathering wealth be hoarding rather than spending, he says, as a consequence of his gathering: ﴿and hoarded (it)﴾, that is, he placed what he had gathered into a container and stored it up out of greed and long hope, and did not give God's right due from it. So his concern was storing it up rather than giving what was obligatory of the right, turning toward this world (p-400) and turning away from the Hereafter.

When it was among the most astonishing of wonders that anyone would turn toward this world while hearing this warning of being presented before Allah and of punishment for those who do not turn toward His worship, He (glory be to Him) made clear that this is because of the disposition He created in him, and that man is overpowered by his disposition, except for whomever Allah protects. This indicates from both sides the greatness of His power, glory be to Him. He spoke with emphasis, since the situation calls for emphasis, because if a person were warned of being presented before some of the rulers, he would avoid doing what angers them. So how about the Mighty, the Wise, the Powerful, the All-Knowing: ﴿Indeed, man﴾, i.e., this species. He expressed it this way because of his familiarity with himself, his seeing of his own good qualities, and his forgetting of his Lord and of his sin.

Since the situation called for explaining the innate disposition that calls to what it requires through its owner's choice, in a manner as if it were compulsion, as a clarification of the ease of matters for Him, glory be to Him, he put into the passive His saying: ﴿was created anxious﴾, i.e., he was formed with a disposition in which he is extremely anxious. That is the most vile impatience, together with intense greed, little patience, stinginess with wealth, and desire for what is not fitting. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it means one who is greedy for what is not lawful to him. It is also narrated from him that its explanation is what follows it.

Since al-halaʿ (haloʿ, extreme anxiety) is intense greed and little patience, he elaborated its meaning and said, placing first the object (maʿmul), which is the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), before the governing verb, to explain how quickly he hastens in that: ﴿When evil touches him﴾ [i.e.] even the slightest touch, ﴿evil﴾ i.e. this kind (of thing), namely whatever harm its sparks scatter, ﴿he becomes distressed﴾ i.e. greatly anguished, which is the opposite of patience, to the point that its bearer almost splits in two and crumbles.

Verse 21: "And when good touches him, he is withholding." (Surah al-Ma'arij, 70:21)

Al-Biqa'i's commentary (Nazm al-Durar):

﴿And when harm touches him﴾, i.e., in that same way, ﴿the good﴾, i.e., this kind [of thing], namely that which suits him and which he specifies, such as abundance in wealth and other kinds of provision, ﴿withholding﴾, i.e., excessive in holding back from what is due from him of rights, out of being immersed in love of the immediate and having his view confined to it, standing fixed on the perceptible because of the predominance of rigidity (judud) and dullness (baladah). This attribute is the opposite of faith, because it [faith] is ﴿two halves﴾: patience (sabr) and gratitude (shukr).

Note on translation: the opening words of the verse, ﴿وإذا مَسَّهُ﴾, are rendered as "And when harm touches him" in the commentary's own gloss, and the line above follows the Arabic text as given; the clause "a man who is" in the verse itself is not present in this excerpt, so the bracketed phrase "[ نِصْفانِ-]" is rendered as "two halves" as it stands in the source.

Since the sense is: "He hastens after what he was created with, of what follows from impatience in matters the Law does not permit, and of what follows from withholding even from that, so he would be among the people of the Fire." And since it is part of perfect power that He, glorified is He, preserves whoever He wills from disgrace despite his natural disposition, and drives him to break his self time after time until what he has of the disposition to evil dissolves, and the spirit remains in its original state, in the primordial nature (fitrah), so that it never ceases urging him to hasten to obey Him, glorified and exalted is He, and to guard His limits, then there is no nobility greater than a responsible person's guarding of the limits of the Law while it runs contrary to his temperament. Thus he combines faith in its two halves: patience and gratitude, since he gathers these eight attributes that lead to the eight gates of Paradise, and they are causes for it. He excepted [min -] from this category the anxious (al-halu'). For this reason he gathered them, saying: (p. 402) ﴿Except those who pray﴾, that is, those who are steadfast in the prayer, which is the place of dependence (on God), and who are deeply rooted in this quality, for their anxiety does not become severe, so their impatience and their withholding are not severe either. Thus they are in the best of forms, balanced, hastening to what pleases the Lord. For He, glorified is He, joined to what He created them with of anxiety the purity of the body alongside the purity of their clay and the cleanness of their spirits, and what He prepared for refining their souls: what He facilitates for them of companions in goodness and friends of kindness, hearing fine admonitions, keeping far from the sources of impurity in places, companions, speech, deeds and all other conditions, and being engaged with everything that carries them to lofty heights of virtuous qualities, until they became among the people of perfection. For this reason He described them with what shows their nobility in that quality, saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 23:

﴿Those who are﴾ i.e., with the entirety of their inner selves and outward conduct, ﴿constant in their prayer﴾ i.e., the prayer which is the greatest part of their religion, and which benefits them and no one else, as indicated by the idafa (construction of possession), and the intended sense is the genus, encompassing all its types, except that the greater part of what is intended is the obligatory prayer. For this reason he expressed it with the noun that denotes permanence, in His saying: ﴿who are constant (da'imun)﴾, i.e., they have no slackening in it and no separation from it; rather they keep to it with such steady adherence that it is judged, by reason of it, that when they are free from it, it is before their eyes, through the constant remembrance of it and readiness to perform it, because it is their connection with their Worshipped One, from whom they have no good except from Him. Thus they are not forgetful of their faults, nor pleased with their virtues. And prayer is sufficient as a blessing in indicating deliverance from this description which necessitates the causes of the Fire. It is an act of worship with conditions, pillars, obligatory parts, forms, [sunan] and etiquettes, opened with the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") and closed with the taslim (saying "as-salamu 'alaykum"). It is divided into that which has bowing (ruku') and prostration (sujud), into that which has prostration without bowing, such as the prostration of gratitude and of recitation, and into that which has neither bowing nor prostration, such as the funeral prayer (salat al-janazah).

When he mentioned the purification of the soul, he followed it with the purification of its counterpart, wealth, saying, clarifying the firmness of the description through the conjunction with "wa" (and): ﴿And those in whose wealth there is a known right﴾, that is, the wealth which He, glory be to Him, bestowed upon them. ﴿A known right﴾. Since the context here is for a more general category than the good-doers who were mentioned earlier in Surat adh-Dhariyat, he restricted it to the obligatory (fard), saying: ﴿known﴾, i.e., from the zakat and all the obligatory (wajiba) expenditures.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 25:

When asking involves lowering one's face and humbling oneself, which calls for compassion, together with protecting one's self and avoiding blame, He placed first His words: ﴿for the beggar﴾, that is, the one who makes an effort to ask for spending, the one who begs. And since among people there are those whose resolve is lofty and whose rank is high, who would not sink into the depths of humiliation by lowering themselves to ask because of poverty, He (said), by way of alerting and discerning those who are attentive to God: ﴿and the deprived﴾, that is, the one who keeps himself chaste (al-mutaʿaffif), (p-404) who does not ask and so is thought to be rich, while he has no wealth to suffice him. He burns with its fire by night and by day, and has no refuge after his Lord, the Owner of his outward and inward affairs, except pouring out his tears in his humility and brokenness. This, from God Most High, is an exhortation to attend to those in dire need, whether those who have no means of earning or those who have become poor after wealth. The righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) excelled in this and similar matters. It is related of Zayn al-ʿAbidin that when he died, dark marks were found on his back when he was washed, like straps. They wondered at them. After some days, widowed women said: "A man used to come to us at night bringing waterskins and sacks of flour on his back, and we lost him [and were in need]." Then they knew that it was he, and that those straps were from that. It is also narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man saw him walking at night during his caliphate, so he followed him until he would know where he was heading. He kept following him until he came to the house of widowed women. He said: "Do you have water, or shall I fill it for you?" They gave him a jar, so he took it and went and filled it on his shoulder and brought it to them. The accounts about them on this subject are many and very famous.

Since wealth may be spent on setting the affairs of this world right, he made clear that the only beneficial part of it is that which attests to faith (al-īmān), so he said: ﴿And those who affirm the Day of Judgment﴾, i.e., who bring about affirmation (al-taṣdīq) toward the one who informs them and renew it at every time, ﴿of the Day﴾. Since the aim is to urge action for the sake of being presented before the Supreme King, he expressed it with His words: ﴿of Recompense﴾, i.e., the requital, the like of which does not exist, which is the Day of Resurrection on which reckoning takes place and accounting is made for the smallest and the slightest. True affirmation of it (ḥaqq al-taṣdīq) is preparation for it through righteous deeds. Those who work for that Day are the ones who act (al-ʿummāl), whereas those who affirm only through mere words will have ruin (al-wabāl), even if they spend the like of mountains.

Since religion (dīn) means recompense, in the form of reward and punishment, and since someone might restrict it to reward alone, knowing that His mercy is all-encompassing and that His mercy overcame His wrath, He stated the punishment explicitly, saying: ﴿And those who are﴾, that is, with all their inner selves, ﴿fearful of the punishment of their Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to them, not of the punishment of anyone else, for the one who does good is more deserving of being feared, even if it were only for the cessation of His goodness. And when He is feared in the station of His beneficence, fear is all the more fitting when He is exalted in the attributes of majesty, such as pride, subjugation and vengeance. ﴿Are apprehensive﴾, that is, they are fearful in this world with a great fear, one that is firmly rooted, lest He punish them in the Hereafter, or in this world, or in both. Therefore they neither become heedless, nor do they do anything except what pleases Him, glorified is He.

(p-406) Since the context calls for instilling fear, he expressed the hope [of reward] for performing acts of obedience by the term "religion" (al-din). Thus the punishment was mentioned twice, by allusion and by explicit statement, and he reinforced it further with his words, as an emphatic parenthetical clause addressing their denial of it: ﴿Indeed, the punishment of their Lord﴾, i.e., the One who nurtured them while they were immersed in His favor, and who they know is able to take retribution, even by withdrawing favor, ﴿is not to be deemed safe﴾, i.e., no one should consider himself safe from it; rather, it is permissible that it befall him even if he has striven greatly in obedience, because the King is Owner and His dominion is complete, so He may do whatever He wills. As for one who permits the occurrence of punishment, he is kept at the greatest distance from its causes, and he has always remained balanced between fear and hope.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 29:

When he mentioned adorning oneself by purifying the soul through prayer and purifying wealth through charity, he urged abandoning (al-takhalli, emptying oneself of) a matter that combines the defiling of wealth and of the soul, namely fornication (zina), which is driven by lust of the private parts (shahwat al-farj), the greatest of desires in driving the soul toward destructive things. So, after mentioning the warning of punishment, he said, to inform that it (fornication) is quicker to befall the one who engages in this filth than a fly is to fall into the sweetest of drinks: ﴿And those who are﴾, that is, with their inner selves, which dominate their outer selves, ﴿guardians of their private parts﴾, that is, whether they are males or females, ﴿[who] guard [them]﴾, that is, guarding them constantly and steadfastly ﴿from everything that Allah has forbidden﴾.

When he had mentioned this preservation in this manner, he mentioned what was permitted in the style of exception, indicating that it is as though he had not mentioned it, and that one only exits after establishing the generality of preservation, not that it is an intended matter from the outset with the aim of describing it. So he said: ﴿except from their spouses﴾, meaning by the contract of marriage (nikah).

When he placed them first for their nobility and the nobility of the offspring through them, he followed it with his saying: ﴿or what﴾. He used the word "what" (ma), which is the more common form for non-rational beings, as a recommendation to widen the scope in accommodating them, ﴿their right hands possess﴾, meaning from the slave-women (sararri), who are the place of tilth and offspring, and who are less in intellect than men.

Since marriage is an act of worship only rarely, and since the basic principle of worship is going beyond habit, and whoever does not dedicate himself to worship would be blameworthy, he suffices in praising him with the negation of blame from him, and he emphasized it because the original state was that he deserved blame for devoting himself to attaining what he desired. So he said, causing it as a consequence of the excepted matter: ﴿for indeed they﴾, meaning because of their turning with their private parts toward these women and removing the veil for that purpose, ﴿are not blameworthy﴾, meaning in enjoying them, from any blamer whatsoever, as he indicated by the passive form. So they keep company with them intending chastity, self-restraint, and seeking offspring, to cooperate in obeying Allah.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 31:

When that which is excluded makes clear the prohibition of everything other than it, and guarding the private parts from it becomes obligatory, he stated it explicitly in a manner that encompasses the preliminaries, so he said, as a consequence of it: ﴿Then whoever seeks﴾, i.e., desires, and he expressed it with the form of ifti'al (ightasa, "seeking"), because that does not occur except from a great inclination of the soul (p-408) and striving in the pursuit ﴿beyond that﴾, i.e., anything of this kind outside this matter which Allah the Exalted has made lawful, and which is the highest of the ranks in the matter of marriage, while the fulfilment of desire is the best and most beautiful of it. And since reaching that does not occur except through the agent's causing it, he linked with the particle fa' (fa, "then") his statement: ﴿then those﴾, i.e., those who are at the lowest depth of baseness and the utmost distance from the places of mercy, ﴿they are﴾, i.e., in their inner selves and their outward conduct, ﴿the transgressors﴾, i.e., those specifically characterized by going beyond the limit that has been permitted.

Now that he had mentioned those who transgress, he followed it with those who stand firm at the limits, saying: ﴿And those who﴾ — that is, by exerting full effort in directing their inner selves — ﴿are faithful to their trusts﴾ — that is, [all] that God has entrusted to them of His right and the right of others.

Since such trusts may exist without a covenant, he specified, saying: ﴿and their covenant﴾ — that is, the trusts that were [among] those bound by speech and confirmed by a pledge — ﴿they keep﴾ — that is, they guard them, acknowledging [them] in a manner that is beneficial and not harmful.

Since the most binding of covenants and trusts are those confirmed by witnessing, He says, explaining the excellence of testimony: ﴿And those who﴾ — that is, with the utmost attentiveness of the heart — ﴿are upright in their testimonies﴾, the testimonies they have given or those they call upon others to give for some claim or other. The placing of the object before the verb indicates that they are so intent upon upholding them and observing them that it is as if they have no other preoccupation besides them (p-409). ﴿Standing firm﴾ — that is, they bear them and discharge them to the utmost completeness and excellence, like one who is prepared for them and stands waiting for their occasion.

When these matters' opposites were deadly deficiencies, and souls, because of the deficiency in them, tend toward deficiencies and incline toward treacheries, He, glory be to Him, mentioned the remedy that cures every disease. He said, indicating the preservation of the states of the prayer (ṣalāh) and its attributes after [ mentioning -] the preservation of its essence and substance, as a warning about the intensity of concern for it: ﴿Those who﴾. When He placed the pronoun in the middle, indicating full devotion with the whole heart, He put the relative clause first, as was done in what has been said, for emphasis and for conveying the meaning to the furthest possible extent, as is not hidden from one with taste. He said: ﴿over their prayer﴾, both the obligatory and the voluntary, ﴿they guard﴾, meaning they go to great lengths in preserving it and renew that preservation, so that it is as if they hasten to preserve it and compete with it in that, so they preserve it because of their own vigilance. Or they compete with others in preserving it for its times, its conditions, its pillars, its completions, outwardly and inwardly, through humility, watchfulness, and the other qualities of excellence (iḥsān). When they perform these, they will inevitably be a restraint for the one who performs them, ﴿that the prayer﴾ when complete ﴿forbids indecency and wrong﴾, so it compels them to all of these commands and keeps them far from their opposites. Because this context concerns the removal of attributes that lead to disbelief, and the limit of the prayer is an indication (p. 410) that obligatory duties suffice for that, though the general sense includes [ ... ], and the context concerns the believers, the people of firm rootedness in good deeds, He combined the two categories: the singular in the first, so that it is directed at the obligatory duties from the outset, and the plural in some readings (qirāʾāt), so that it also includes the voluntary prayers (nawāfil) in their various kinds. Opening the attributes with the prayer and closing them with it is, in the clarification of its majesty and greatness, a striking matter.

When he had described their qualities, he followed it with what He had bestowed upon them. He said, beginning a new sentence and drawing a conclusion without a connecting *fa'* (fa), to indicate that His mercy is what brought them to this state, though in reality they had no cause of their own: ﴿Those are﴾, that is, those who are at the highest degree of elevation because of these lofty qualities they possess. He expressed it in a way that indicates that He, glory be to Him, hastened their reward, and said: ﴿in gardens﴾, that is, in this world and the Hereafter. As for the Hereafter, this is clear. As for this world, it is because, having striven in these qualities by wearing out their souls until they took on their character, He granted them, through experiencing them, delights of the intimacy of nearness and the sweetness of intimate conversation with Him, to which nothing is comparable at all. The Garden is a place in which all comforts, pleasures and joys are gathered, and from which all disliked things and evils are removed. Its opposite is the Fire. He added to this by saying: ﴿honored﴾, using the passive participle to indicate the generality of honor from the Creator and from creatures who speak and others, because He, glory be to Him, decreed that their rank be exalted so that they would be the greatest in personal distinction for them in the Unseen, while being greatly honored when they are face to face, so that they would have a share in the creation of their Prophet (ﷺ).

On the day of Banu Qurayza, 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who had preceded him to them, met him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, what prevents you from not approaching these wicked people?" He said: "And why? Perhaps you heard some harm from them concerning me. If I had approached them, they would not have said anything of that sort." Then he approached them and said: "Has Allah disgraced you, O brothers of the apes and the swine?" They said: "Be quiet, O Abu al-Qasim, you were not ignorant!" and they spoke to him in the best manner they could. Likewise, Quraysh was with him before the Hijra in most of his circumstances. This is regarding this world. As for the Hereafter, the angels will receive them with glad tidings at the time of death, in their graves, and from the time they rise from their graves until the time they enter their palaces.

When this divine discourse had been established, which no sensible person doubts is beyond the power of any created being, and that none can do it except God, the One who has no partner, who knows all things and has power over all things, then (it is established) that no one can overcome the deficiencies of humanity and emerge from the darkness of deficiency into the light of excellence except one who adheres to these attributes and purifies his soul by them, so that he becomes [complete]. Together with the certain knowledge, shared by Muslim and disbeliever alike, that perfection is the cause of happiness, and that man is disposed toward [what] He, glory be to Him, has described of deficiencies, he knew that those who possess these attributes are the ones specially destined for the happiness of the Hereafter. The disbelievers used to come to the Prophet ﷺ and sit close around him in order to hear his words, to deny him and to mock him. A sensible person should not come to anything, especially if his coming to it is in the manner of hastening, except to obtain happiness. On this basis He said, expressing the greatness of the Qur'an, with a meaning that amounts to this: when they hear it, they become, because of the intensity of what its matter frightens them, unable to control themselves, and they act like one who has lost his senses: ﴿So what is [wrong] with those who disbelieve﴾, that is, what share of happiness is there for those who have covered the mirrors of their minds against acknowledging the content of this discourse, which is clearer than the sun, while they are ﴿before you﴾, that is, toward you, O noble Messenger, and facing what is turned toward you, ﴿hastening﴾, that is, rushing, with ﴿stretched necks﴾ and continuous gazing at you, in extreme wonder at your speech, with the awe of one who strives toward a matter without which he has no life.

Since the one who takes omens and observes the right and the left, as was mentioned in Surat al-Saffat, does not leave off doing so except in a matter that has bewildered his mind and stripped away his reason, so that he is not left to reflect, He said, indicating the intensity of their eagerness for this headlong rush while taking no precaution against anything: ﴿Ein﴾, meaning, coming at you from every direction, ﴿from the right﴾, meaning from you, where they hope for good omen by it, ﴿and from the left﴾, meaning from you, even though they take bad omen by it, ﴿in groups﴾, meaning, while they are gathered in bands upon bands and crowds upon crowds, scattered into sects, divided into parties, going at a measured pace so that they may come all together as a single assembly. Its root is ʿizwah (a band, a faction), because each group is affiliated (ta'tazi) to something other than what the other group is affiliated to; it was pluralized by the sound masculine plural (jamʿ salamah) irregularly (shudhudhan).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 38:

Since this hastening in this manner should only occur regarding that which is certainly felicitous, and with the certainty that it is felicitous, it should only be for that through which eternal happiness is attained; (al-Biqa'i) said, drawing attention to this and denouncing that there should be for them what should only be for Him, given that their doing this was among their mockery: when they gathered to listen to what he recited, they would say: "If what he says is true, about the resurrection and Paradise, we will surely be happier with it than them [just as I am happier than them] in this world," as Allah the Exalted said, relating about them in His saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, surely I shall have the best with Him﴾ [Fussilat: 50]. This is because error often arises when a person is in good in this world, so he thinks that this is a barrier between him and the Fire, because it is good in reality; or he thinks that Allah's granting him respite while he is upon falsehood means that He is pleased with it, and he does not realize that only one who fears losing something becomes distressed, anxious and hasty. [Or that something happens without his will.] ﴿Does every one of them aspire﴾, that is, with this coming. He expressed it with "aspire" as an indication that they reached the utmost limit of foolishness, since they sought the most precious things without any cause they had engaged in for it.

Since their coming was in the form of dispersal, without waiting for one group to join another, He said: ﴿every one of them﴾, that is, individually. Since what is desired is entry into the Garden and not its being from a specific gate, He said, using the passive voice: ﴿to be admitted﴾, that is, by hastening in disbelief, while being a disbeliever without a faith that purifies him, just as the Muslim is admitted, so that the wrongdoer and the doer of good are not equal, ﴿into a Garden of bliss﴾, that is, in which there is nothing but bliss in all that is in it, as far as its extent is concerned.

Since the sense of the rhetorical interrogative that implies negation has been established, and it does not enter (into the matter), He reinforced that with the conveying of irritation and belittlement, by bringing the "mother of rebukes and deterrents," so He said: ﴿Never!﴾ That is, what they hope for will not come about at all, because that is a vain wish with no cause behind it, as indicated by the use of the word "greed" (tama') rather than "hope" (raja').

Since a person who excessively engages in something and makes it his habit, it becomes acceptable among them to say: "So-and-so was created from such-and-such," He explained this with His words, emphasizing and singling them out as deniers, because they, despite knowing their own deficiency, claim perfection: ﴿Indeed We﴾, with the majesty We possess, ﴿have created them﴾ with a power that no one can withstand, so that one would divert any part of his will from the direction toward which He has directed it to another ﴿from what they know﴾ (p. 415). That is, from what one is ashamed to mention, in essence and in meaning. As for the essence, it is a foul drop of semen, expelled from the place of urine, and We nourished it with menstrual blood; from it issue urine and filth. As for the meaning, it is the restlessness, the impatience, and the stinginess, which they themselves agree are deficiencies. Thus they are not fit for the abode of perfection except by purifying their souls from these traits mentioned earlier, which the Exalted King urged upon them. Al-Baghawi related with his chain of narration from Bishr ibn Jihash (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "He spat once into His palm, placed His finger upon it, and said: 'The Mighty and Majestic says: Son of Adam! How can you escape Me when I created you from the like of this? Until when I had made you complete and proportioned you, you walked between two cloaks, and the earth was yours to walk on gently; you gathered and withheld. Until when it reached the collarbones, you said: "I will give charity," and when is the time of charity?'" — End.

When the mention of this creation, together with what precedes it, is a great indication of what they used to say, namely that if the matter were as they claim, regarding resurrection and Paradise, "we will surely be more favoured with God than you, and we will surely enter it, just as we are now more favoured than you [in His sight] by the wealth we possess, the ease of our worldly life, and our standing and prosperity," and as a warning that [all] are equal in that they are all from a drop of semen, so their superiority in this world through these visible blessings is from none but Him, glorified is He, while He has favoured the believers with the inner blessings, which, in their firm possession of them, increased them in purification through these practical attributes arising from the cognitive attribute. He is able to add the outward blessings to the inner blessings. For this reason He made His saying the consequence of this: He emphasized it by negating an oath, which indicates that there is no need for it, because of the abundance of proofs that dispense with it, given the strangeness of what is sworn to at that time, due to the multitude of disbelievers and the strength of their power: ﴿So no﴾, meaning, as a consequence of Our creating them and of that warning, which shows that We are able to do everything We will and that nothing can overpower Us, that is, "No, ﴿I swear﴾." He therefore turned the speech to the singular pronoun, free of the manifestation of majesty, lest an obstinate person be captious about the matter of divine oneness. ﴿By the Lord﴾, meaning the Nourisher, Master, Originator, and Governor, ﴿of the easts﴾ where the sun, the moon, and the wandering planets rise each day from a point among them, according to the method He ordained and the sound law He perfected and subjected, six months ascending and six months descending. ﴿And the wests﴾ likewise, according to this firmly ordered arrangement that admits no disorder, and from which arise the night and the day and the four seasons. Thus the welfare of the world depends on knowing reckoning, on the proper provision of food and drink, and on other needs. Thus each of the two alternations comes into being after it was not, and the plants, from the star and the tree, follow the same continuous custom, indicating that He is able to originate and annihilate everything He wills in the manner He wills, without any effort whatsoever.

Since the meaning is: "I do not swear by that, although it is great, because the matter is so clear that it needs no oath, just as if one adversary said to another, 'Swear,' and he replied, 'The matter is too evident for my oath, for only one who has no proof needs to swear; then I bring proofs that leave no room for doubt.'" And since they, while acknowledging God's power, were in their claim of their own superiority like those who deny the power to reverse the matter, He emphasized His saying, returning to the manifestation of majesty, after removing the confusion with what is clearer than the sun: ﴿Indeed We﴾, meaning with the majesty that is Ours, ﴿are surely able﴾, with kinds of emphasis: by the particle, by the nominal sentence, and by the turn to the manifestation of majesty in both the subject and the predicate. Thus in His informing after the oath, together with the emphasis, there is an indication of the highest degrees of emphasis.

ﷺ

﴿Upon that We are able to replace them﴾ [meaning: with] a great replacement, with the majesty that We possess, as a substitute for them, ﴿with those better than them﴾, i.e., in creation; or a change of attribute, so that they would be greater in expansiveness in this world, more abundant in wealth, children, higher in rank, greater in dignity, prestige, resolve, and servants. They would then be a people of one heart before You in listening to your words, honoring you, magnifying you, and striving in everything that would gladden your heart, in place of what these people do of mockery, clapping, whistling, and everything that constricts your breast. God, glorified is He, did precisely this with the Emigrants, the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness: with abundance of provision through taking the wealth of the tyrants of Kisra and Caesar, and with firm establishment in the land, until they became the kings of this world, while acting in ways that entitle them to the kingdom of the Hereafter. So they sought to relieve the distress of the Messenger of God ﷺ and expended in pursuit of his pleasure their souls and their wealth.

Since a person may do something and then regret it, He informed that He, glorified is He, is other than that, and so He said: ﴿And We are not﴾. He emphasized the matter with the nominal form situated in the manifestation of greatness, so He said: ﴿We﴾, and He intensified the negation, so He said: ﴿outrun﴾, i.e., by any preceding thing that overcomes something We did not intend in any way whatsoever; and for this reason He used the passive participle.

When it was established that He, glory be to Him, possesses supreme and dazzling greatness through the all-encompassing scope of His knowledge and the perfection of His power, and this produced the reliance of the people of His party upon Him and their turning away from everything other than Him, He made the following statement a consequence of that. It is both a threat to the opponents and a consolation to the allies: ﴿So leave them﴾, that is, leave them [ even if -] in their worst condition, ﴿to plunge (yakhūḍū)﴾, that is, to engage in their speech and their actions, none of which is done with mastery. Rather, it is like the conduct of one who wades into water without placing his foot where he knows it will please him, so he is in danger (p-419) of falling or drowning. ﴿And to play (yalʿabū)﴾, that is, to act like one at play, whose action has no benefit except the waste of time and neglect of what matters greatly.

Since what God has promised concerning the conditions of the Hereafter must certainly occur, it is as if it is coming toward the human being while the human being strives with his effort toward it. Therefore He expressed it with the form of mutual action (mufāʿala) and said: ﴿until they meet﴾ (yulāqū). Since what befalls the disbelievers from it is greatest, that day is as if it belongs specifically to them, so He said: ﴿their day which﴾. Since the warning (waʿīd), which is the report of something said in order to frighten the one being threatened, is piercing to hearts when it comes from the One who is able and without any need to mention the one threatened, He used the passive form in His words: ﴿they are promised (yūʿadūna)﴾. It is the day of the lifting of the veil, whose beginning is its manifestation at the moment of the death-rattle (ghargharah), and whose end is the second blast of the trumpet, when each of the two groups enters its abode and its place of settlement.

The verse is abrogated (mansūkhah) by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 43:

When what follows the second blast was greater and more terrifying, He replaced it with [His saying]: ﴿The Day they come forth﴾, meaning these people who ask about it mockingly and deem it far-fetched. The reading of Abu Bakr from 'Asim with the passive voice (bi'l-bina' li'l-maf'ul), in the manner of speech of those who have power, indicates that it is something very easy: ﴿from the graves﴾, meaning the tombs in which they have become hidden, under the trampling of the hoof and the shoe, so they are in a state where they cannot repel anything done to them, but are rather like meat in the mouth of one who chews. For the jadath (grave) is the tomb, and al-jadathah is the sound of the hoof and the shoe and the chewing of meat. ﴿Hastening﴾, meaning toward the sound of the Caller.

When it was the habit of a person to hasten toward the markers that are set up for what he intends, and their particular habit is to rush toward the idols (anṣab) which they hold in low regard, out of lightness in knowledge and folly in judgment, He said: ﴿As if they were rushing to a target (nusub)﴾, meaning a set-up marker, with the form being a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, as you say: "This is the object of my eye" and "The emir struck" (this is according to the reading of the majority with a fatha; according to the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Hafs with a damma: toward a sign or a thing they worship besides Allah, with what is in it of deadly disease and affliction, or a stone upon which they slaughter). In al-Jam' bayn al-'Ubab wa'l-Muhkam he said: al-nasb, al-nusb and al-nusub: the disease and the affliction; and al-nusub is everything set up and made into a sign; al-nasb and al-nasab: the raised sign; al-nusb and al-nusub: everything worshipped besides Allah, the plural being anṣab, and the anṣab were stones around the Ka'bah which were set up, over which the name was invoked and upon which slaughter was made for other than Allah; and anṣab al-haram: its boundaries. Abu Hayyan said: al-nasb is what is set up for a person, so that he intends it hastening toward it, whether a sign, a building, or an idol, and it became predominant for idols, until it was said: the anṣab. ﴿They hasten﴾, meaning they hurry with the haste of one who goes toward what pleases him, until it is as if he is darting toward it, just as they used to hasten toward their anṣab.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 70, verse 44:

Since their rushing toward the idols (anṣāb) was in a state of joy, He informed that this is contrary to that, and that the mention of the idols and the depiction of the state of their coming to them was only mockery of them. So He said: ﴿Humbled﴾, i.e., broken and abased, owing to the humiliation and degradation that has befallen them. He attached the feminine marker to it, adding to this meaning and emphasizing it, by saying: ﴿their eyes﴾.

Since their humility is constant, He expressed it with the noun form. And since their abasement increases every moment, He expressed it with the present tense verb, which indicates renewal and continuity, saying: ﴿Will cover them﴾, i.e., will overtake them and envelop them, and will bear down upon them, imposing on them every hardship and constriction, hastening toward them. ﴿Humiliation﴾, the opposite of what they were in this world, because whoever exalted himself in this world against the truth will be humbled in the Hereafter, and whoever humbled himself to the truth in this world will be exalted in the Hereafter.

When He depicted it in this manner, He indicated that what the intellects can grasp of its description is not all of it, and that it is greater than that. So He said: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the matter which is at the utmost height of rank in greatness, ﴿is the Day which they were﴾, i.e., in the state of the world, at the utmost of power in threatening.

Since a threat is only realized when it comes from one who is able, and when it is so, it is frightening and painful even without mentioning the one from whom it issued, the verb ﴿they were promised﴾ is put in the passive. That is, He renews the promise of it to them in this world at every time, perhaps they will take heed, so their hearts soften and they return from the tyranny in which they are. This is the time of the punishment about which they asked at the beginning of the surah. Thus its last part has returned upon its first, as you see, in the most complete return, and its joint has been joined to what connects it, like the joining of the single to the collective. And Allah is the Guide to the right.
